messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 41
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: South Asian
  relationship_status: In a relationship
  occupation: Park Ranger
  trauma_type: Captivity
  pcl5: 40

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Military Topics: Talks about military, Self-Consciousness: Being seen, Authority Figures: People in uniform
  Maladaptive Strategies: Restrict Eating: control eating strictly to feel in control, Revenge Fantasies: I imagine getting revenge on the people responsible, People Pleasing: go along with whatever others want to feel safe
  Threat: Flashbacks: Suddenly feeling or acting as if the stressful experience were actually happening again, Cannot Trust Safety: Even when others tell me I am safe I find it impossible to believe it, Startle to Movement: Unexpected movement nearby causes me to react as if I am in danger
  Memory: Snapshot Memory: I remember the frightening event as a few moments, and each moment is a picture in my mind., Pain Recall: When the memory returns I feel physical pain in the same parts of my body as during the event, Emotionless Recall: Sometimes I can recall what happened but feel completely numb, as if it happened to a stranger
  Negative Appraisals: Isolation: I feel isolated and set apart from others, Humiliation: I feel permanently humiliated by what happened, Self-Comparison: Somebody else would not have gotten into this situation

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Rohan, a 41-year-old park ranger, sits with a stillness that seems at odds with the tension in his shoulders. It has been eighteen months since the solo trekking trip that he now refers to only as "that time." He had been hiking in a remote mountain range, an experienced outdoorsman seeking solitude, when he was taken by a local militia. They mistook him for a foreign operative. The memory of it doesn't arrive as a continuous narrative, but as a slideshow of stark, silent images: the rough texture of the burlap sack pulled over his head, the worn-out insignia on a soldier's uniform, the specific crack in the ceiling of the room where they held him. Sometimes, when he tries to recall the sequence of events, he feels nothing at all, a profound numbness that makes him feel like he’s recounting a story about a stranger.

His captors wore uniforms, and now the sight of any official attire—a police officer at a traffic stop, a security guard at the mall, even his own crisp National Park Service uniform—sends a jolt of ice through him. At work, in the vast wilderness he once considered his sanctuary, he feels constantly exposed. He has come to believe that the park visitors are watching him, judging his every move, their gazes a silent accusation. This feeling of being seen is a direct echo of the interrogation room, where he was forced to stand for hours under the unblinking stare of his captors. He is certain that a stronger, smarter person would never have been so naive as to hike in that region alone; this self-reproach is a constant, quiet hum beneath his daily thoughts. What happened feels less like a misfortune and more like a permanent stain of humiliation he can never wash away.

In the months after his release, Rohan’s life began to shrink. He developed habits he didn't understand at first. To regain a sense of control that was stripped from him, he began to restrict his eating with rigid precision, weighing every portion and counting every calorie. The gnawing hunger was a feeling he could command, unlike the terror. At night, when sleep wouldn't come, he would lie awake and construct elaborate revenge fantasies, imagining himself powerful and his captors helpless. These thoughts provided a fleeting surge of strength but left him exhausted and agitated by morning. With his partner and his colleagues, he found himself becoming excessively agreeable, nodding along to any suggestion and suppressing his own needs. It felt safer to be compliant, to offer no resistance, to simply go along with whatever others wanted. He just wanted to feel safe, and he could no longer trust that he was, even when his partner held him and told him he was home.

His body remembers the trauma in ways his mind sometimes doesn't. A few weeks ago, while on patrol, a deer suddenly bolted from the undergrowth. Rohan didn't just jump; he dropped to the ground, his heart hammering against his ribs as if he were under attack. When a memory-image of a guard’s face flashes into his mind, he often feels a ghost of a sharp, radiating pain in his side, right where a boot once connected. These moments are disorienting, visceral intrusions that make the past feel terrifyingly present. He feels utterly set apart from everyone he knows, isolated by an experience he cannot adequately explain and which they could never truly understand.

It was an incident at the park’s visitor center that finally compelled him to seek help. A tourist, a veteran wearing a military-style jacket, began asking him detailed questions about patrol routes and park security. Rohan froze, the man’s authoritative tone transporting him back to the interrogation room. He felt the floor tilt beneath him, the sounds of the center fading into a dull roar. He was there, and he was here, and the terror was absolute. He managed to excuse himself, but the episode left him shaken for days. He is terrified of losing his job, the one piece of his old life he has clung to. More than that, he is afraid that this broken, watchful version of himself is all he will ever be.
